A Little Rock dispatch of Monday says: "George M. Street, one of the most prominent citizens of the state has probably committed suicide in St. Louis His body has not been recovered, but the circumstances attending his disappearance are conclusive, and even his wife has given up all hopes of ever seeing him alive.

The first information received by any one was a letter to Murray Tavlor, in charge of Mr. Street's store at Argenta, which came last Thursday, the 9th instant. This letter was written on the 7th and mailed on the night of the 8th, near the Southern Hotel, in St. Louis. It was stamped "St. Louis, Aug. 9, 1:30 a. m."

In this letter Mr. Street says he will commit suicide by drowning in the Mississippi river before the letter reaches here. At the same time he wrote his wife at Dalton, Ga., and wrote J. H. Harrod here to take charge of his business and do the best he could for his wife and children and his creditors. Mrs. Street got there Saturday night and found his room at the Southern Hotel just as he had left it, and containing his valise, clothing and umbrella. He had not been seen since Wednesday night.

Mr. Stteet has recently met with financial reverses, and in a condition of temporary insanity has no doubt taken his life. The police at St. Louis have been requested to use every ef fort to find his body, and a reward has been offered for its recovery.

Mr. Street left Little Rock July 26, going to St. Louis, his wife having left a few days previously for Dalton, Ga., to visit relatives. For some weeks his friends had observed that he appeared greatly depressed in spirits, and it was known that he had been playing the races heavily. He was in partnership with Paul J. Miles, the noted race horse owner, and some of thn horses are now in New York in the name of Miles & Street.

After receiving the letter addressed to her in which he discussed his condition and intentions at some length, Mrs Street went at once to St. Louis and found that his room at the hotel was just as he had left it, and there was no trace whatever of him. Mrs. Street returned today fully convinced of her husband's death. She was appointed by Judge Mills this morning administratrix of the estate and has taken charge of the property.

The dead man leaves his wife, to whom he has been married only two years, and two almost grown daughters by his first wife, who live with their grand-mother at Rienzi, Miss. His financial interests are said to be heavily involved. In his letters he said that he was overwhelmed with financial reverses and was unable to face his friends, with whom he had always borne a good reputation. His act was deliberate, but many believe that his mind had become unbalanced through continued brooding over his troubles,

Geooge M. Street came to Little Rock in January, 1887, without capital. He secured a position as prescription clerk in the drug store of C. J. Humphreys. This position he held until June 1888. He established the Argenta Mercantile Company that year and was made secretary and manager. In 1890 he was elected secretary of the Argenta Building and Loan Association. He was considered a heavy better on the horses, and has been known to win and lose as much as $10,000 on a single race.

Mr. Street was active in politics and was chairman of the Democratic county central committee. A special meeting has been called by Secretary F. G. Ginocchio for Thursday at 10 a. m., to elect his successor in that position.

Reidsville, August 24.—News reached here at 5 o'clock this afternoon of a criminal assault upon the 6-year-old daughter of John H. Huskey, who lives six miles west of Reidsville. The crime was committed by Joe Scales, a negro boy 15 years old.

The crime was discovered by the mother of the girl. Hearing the screams of her daughter and being told by her younger children the cause, the mother secured a revolver and ran after the negro. He ran into a barn and took refuge under a wagon. Mrs. Huskey forced him to come out, and at the point of the pistol marched him to the house; then she rang the farm bell for the men in the fields.

They came at once and also friends from adjoining farms, hearing the alarm, were soon on the spot. They seized the boy, bound him, and carried him to Wentworth before Magistrate J. G. Mitchell. After the magistrate's trial he was committed to pail. Much excitement is felt over the affair, but the youth of the negro will prevent his lynching.

WHIPPING BOSS'S FATAL WORK.

Death of a Convict After Great Brutality—An Indictment Found.

Indictment Found.

ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 2.—Because of the death of George Bankston, a convict, shortly after being whipped severely, the Grand Jury of Bartow county has indicted A. T. Tomlinson, the whipping boss at the Sugar Hill mining camp, for manslaughter. In the early part of June it is alleged that Bankston became ill and complained that he was unable to work. Tomlinson, the whipping boss, believing he was playing off, administered ten lashes with a leather strap three inches wide. In the afternoon Bankston again refused to work and got eighteen lashes with the strap. The next morning he still failed to work and Tomlinson gave him another whipping, this time applying fifty lashes. When the afternoon came Bankston still asserted that he was unable to work and he was whipped again, sixty lashes being applied.

The next morning Bankston died. The Grand Jury of Bartow got wind of the affair and a true bill was returned against Tomlinson, charging him with involuntary manslaughter.

The Indians were surprised several days ago by a force of 2,000 Government troops, who attacked their right flank. After a stubborn resistance the Mayas retreated a short distance to a stronger defensive position, which they held with great persistence and bravery. It is charged that the Mayas are led by several Englishmen, supposed to be from British Honduras.

Officer Henry Messer, while attempting to arrest a negro was attacked and compelled to open fire on the crowd.

Akron, O., Aug 23.—A mob took possession of this city last evening and one boy was shot dead, and several persons were wounded in the rioting. It all arose over a negro. On Monday night a negro named Louis Peck made an attempt to asasult Christina, a 6-year-old daughter of Mr and Mrs Theodore Maas, white people of this city. The negro was arrested at 1 o'clock yesterday morning and locked up in the city prison. At 7:30 o'clock last night a mob of several thousand persons gathered about the city prison yelling for the life of Peck. They forced their way into the city prison and searched all the cells. The officers offered no resistance, as the negro had been removed in the early part of the evening. The mob then rushed for the county jail and forced open the outer doors of the building. The jail was soon packed with the howling members of the mob, who insisted that Peck was there.

Deputy Sheriff Stone addressed the mob, saying that Peck was not there. A committee was appointed by the mob and was permitted to search the jail from top to bottom. The mob then rushed across the street and forced open the doors of the court house and searched that building. Peck was not there and then another rush was made for the city prison, which was again soon packed.

The officers made no resistance and Mayor Young appeared at a window in the upper part of the building and attempted to address the crowd. He told the people that Peck and another negro named "Bug" Howard, who was arrested two weeks ago for shooting a white man, were removed from the city by Sheriff Kelly. At 4 o'clock he took the two colored prisoners to Cleveland for safe keeping.

The mob attacked the city building for the third time soon after 10 o'clock. People in the crowd opened fire on the building and it was returned by the police officers in the building. One boy was shot dead and several people wounded. Mayor Young at midnight made preparations to call out the militia.

Shortly after midnight the mob broke into a hardware store and stole all the firearms and ammunition they could find, including guns, rifles and revolvers, and proceeded to the city building and opened fire on the defenders, and finally set fire to the Columbia hall, which adjoins the city building. Cleveland, O., Aug. 24.—This afternoon, Peck, the Akron negro, with Prison Keeper Washer, Dr. A. K. Akron, O., Aug. 24.—Just after leaving Cuyahoga Falls, while the train was en route from Cleveland to Akron, Peck begged Prison Keeper Washer to shoot him instantly in the event a mob was waiting at Akron. The plans made contemplated leaving the train at the union station at Akron. Peck's fright increased as the train neared Akron. He begged piteously to be shot if a mob threatened. Washer did not consent.

The train carrying Peck arrived here at 3:30 p. m. A carriage was waiting at the railway station and Peck was quickly bundled into it. In three minutes the court house was reached and Peck was arraigned before Judge Nye. The indictment was read. Peck stood up and plead guilty. He declared he had nothing to say, except that he threw himself upon the mercy of the court. The court then sentenced Peck to life imprisonment in the state penitentiary. Troops were on guard at the railway station and along the route to the court house. There was no demonstration whatever. After Peck had ben sentenced he was at once taken in a closed carriage to the Center street crossing of the Cleveland, Akron and Columbus railway and placed on board the train in a train in charge of Sheriff Kelly and taken on to the state penitentiary at Columbus. So quickly and quietly was Peck brought into the city, sentenced and sent on to Columbus that but few people knew what had transpired. There was no crowd at the railway station either when the train arrived or departed. Few who glanced at the rapidly driven carriage suspected that it contained the man the furlous mob of Wednesday night wanted to lynch.

Peck was taken in at the rear door of the court house. There was a stir among the soldiers, crowding the rear of the court room. Judge D. J. Nye of Elyria, presided. He arrived at Akron at noon today. Two minutes aftertet Peck reached the court Deputy Sheriff Ed Hersey read the indictment. Peck stood up with manacled hands. He pleaded guilty in a firm voice. His worn eyes shifted nervously about the room. Then he sat down and Prosecutor Wanamaker whispered with him briefly. Then Judge Nye said:

"Mr. Peck, you have heard the indictment read, charging you with rape. You have plead guilty. Have you anything to say?"

"I have nothing to say except that I throw myself on the mercy of the court," replied Mr. Peck.

RIOTERS AT A CIRCUS.
Colored Men Attack a Special Officer in Hyndman. Pa.
CUMBERLAND, Md., Aug. 22. — Colored rioters terrorized the town of Hyndman, Pa., on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, fourteen miles northwest of Cumberland Monday night and yesterday morning. At least a hundred of them marched through the streets howling and demanding the blood of William Baldwin, a white man, who until recently was a foreman over the negroes who are working on the excavation for the Baltimore and Ohio track.

The negroes had been paid off, and a circus being at Hyndman, all proceeded there and were drinking. Baldwin, who is a powerful man, had been in the meantime appointed a special policeman. One of the negroes insulted him, and, as he attempted to arrest him, another negro took Baldwin's pistol out of his pocket, but Baldwin was too quick, and felled him with a club, and then kicked him into insensibility. The crowd closed in on Baldwin, and he disabled seven out of nine.

The negro first attacked is nearly dead, being still unconscious. Baldwin knocked out another negro's eye with a rock. The negro was accused of trying to commit assault on a white woman.

Baldwin is a native Virginian. The negroes are from the vicinity of Washington and Baltimore. A riot nearly ensued when several were arrested yesterday and lodged in jail. The negroes are still very threatening.

A colored man with his head badly crushed, supposedly by a train, was placed in the hospital at Cumberland yesterday in an unconscious condition. He belonged to the gang of workers from which the rioters came.
